newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pledges all-out push to ratify chemical pact.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pledges all-out push to ratify chemical pact.

text.p: The U.S. government's arms control chief on Friday pledged an all-out effort by the second Clinton administration to gain Senate ratification of the Chemical Weapons Convention before an April deadline.

Hungary last week became the 65th country to ratify the convention, signed in 1993, meaning it will automatically go into force next April 29. Any country that has not ratified it by then will be excluded from a role in administering it.

The White House thought the Senate would ratify it in September, but when Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole joined opponents of the treaty, the administration, fearing defeat, agreed a vote should be put off until next year.

Arms Control and Disarmament Agency (ACDA) director John Holum said the administration would resume efforts to get the treaty ratified as soon as the new Congress convenes in January following President Clinton's re-election Tuesday.
"This is a top legislative priority of the administration. It's something that needs to be done quickly, so we need action early in the year," Holum told reporters.
The convention bans production, stockpiling and use of poison gases. It gives countries which have chemical weapon stocks, such as the United States, 10 years to destroy them.

But conservative Republicans mounted a powerful campaign against the pact, saying it would not stop states like Iraq, Iran and North Korea from acquiring chemical weapons and would impose a host of regulations on thousands of U.S. companies.

If the United States does not become an "original party" by ratifying before April 29, it will be excluded from a Hague-based organization that will implement the pact and it will have to accept decisions taken by other countries.

Holum said failure to ratify would also put at risk a "substantial portion" of a $60 billion U.S. chemical export business because of restrictions on trade with non-member countries imposed by the convention.

Pointing out that it was negotiated by former Republican President George Bush, Holum said "there could be no better candidate" than the pact for the Republican Senate leadership to prove its proclaimed wish to work with the administration.
Holum said he expected Clinton would take a personal interest in the issue. "The President has been personally involved and I expect that that will continue," he said.

"Certainly we will have a difficult time with it, but I think now that we have the clock ticking, and everybody will recognize that this is something that needs to be done in the national interest...there is nothing to be gained any longer by making this a political argument," he added.

Administration officials argue that small U.S. companies will not be affected by inspections and other regulations contained in the convention, and that large companies that will be affected support the treaty.
Holum said he expected that the government of Russia, which has also not ratified the convention, would also now make a push to get it through the Duma (parliament).

The United States and Russia are the world's only declared holders of chemical weapons, and Holum said it "would be very uncomfortable and in fact damaging to the treaty if the two countries ... were not original parties".

The United States holds about 30,000 tons of chemical weapons and Russia about 40,000. U.S. officials say Russia is holding back on ratifying partly out of concerns over the cost of destroying stocks, estimated by Moscow at between $4 billion and $6 billion.
